checkpoints.title: Core particles
checkpoints.subtitle: は, が, か, に, で, and more

points.title: ちゃいけない・じゃいけない
points.blurb: Japanese has several ways to tell someone they shouldn't do something — from a parent scolding a child to a formal workplace rule. This lesson covers the casual, spoken end: the kind you'd hear from a friend, a parent, or in everyday conversation. You'll recognize it when someone sets a boundary and know when to say "you shouldn't" versus "you must not."

formation.title: Build from the て-form
formation.body:
Take the verb's て-form and drop て. Add ちゃ or じゃ, then いけない or ダメ.

たべる → たべて → たべちゃ + いけない

formation.title: ちゃ vs じゃ
formation.body:
If the て-form ends in で, use じゃ instead of ちゃ.

のむ → のんで → のんじゃ + いけない

examples.japanese: 寝る前にスマホを見ちゃいけない。
examples.romaji: neru mae ni sumaho o micha ikenai.
examples.english: You shouldn't look at your smartphone before going to bed.

scenario.setting: At home — a parent and child settle in before bed.

lines.speaker: Child
lines.japanese: あと5分だけスマホ見ていい？
lines.romaji: ato go-fun dake sumaho mite ii?
lines.english: Can I look at my phone for just five more minutes?

lines.speaker: Parent
lines.japanese: だめよ。もう遅いでしょ。

examples.japanese: 寝る前にスマホを見ちゃダメよ。
examples.romaji: neru mae ni sumaho o micha dame yo.
examples.english: You shouldn't look at your smartphone before going to bed.

scenario.setting: Same bedtime scene — a softer, everyday warning.

lines.speaker: Child
lines.japanese: ねえ、もう一回だけ見たい。
lines.english: Hey, I just want to check it one more time.

lines.speaker: Parent
lines.japanese: もう遅いのに、まだスマホ？
lines.english: It's late — you're still on your phone?

examples.japanese: 入っちゃだめみたいよ。
examples.english: Looks like we're not supposed to go in.

scenario.setting: Two friends at a hot spring town spot a roped-off steaming pool.

lines.speaker: A
lines.japanese: ねえ、あそこ入っていこうか？
lines.english: Hey, wanna go in over there?

lines.speaker: B
lines.japanese: いや、ちょっと柵があるでしょ。
lines.romaji: iya, chotto saku ga aru desho.

examples.japanese: やっちゃいけないことをやっちゃった。
examples.english: I did something I shouldn't have...

lines.speaker: Friend
lines.japanese: どうしたの？元気ないね。
lines.english: What's wrong? You don't look so good.

lines.english: Yeah… I got yelled at by the teacher.

examples.japanese: 20歳未満の人はお酒を飲んじゃいけません。
examples.romaji: hatachi miman no hito wa osake o nonja ikemasen.

lines.speaker: Customer

drills.instruction: Pick the correct casual prohibition form.

drills.exampleJapanese: 野菜を食べるまでデザートを食べちゃいけないよ。
choices: No dessert until you eat your vegetables.
You may eat dessert before vegetables.
drills.correctChoice: No dessert until you eat your vegetables.
それを食べちゃいけない

choices: そんなに授業をさぼっちゃダメよ。
そんなに授業をさぼってもいいよ。
授業をさぼりたいですか。
drills.correctChoice: そんなに授業をさぼっちゃダメよ。

formation.title: て-form + はいけない
formation.body:
Attach はいけない to the verb's て-form.

かく → かいて → かいてはいけない

formation.title: では for で
formation.body:
When the て-form is で, は often becomes では.

のむ → のんで → のんではいけない

usage.title: Standard prohibition
usage.body: Neutral-to-formal "must not." Common in rules, instructions, and textbooks.

usage.title: Compared to ちゃいけない
usage.body: Same meaning as ちゃいけない, but less casual. Use てはいけない in writing and polite speech.

examples.japanese: ここで写真を撮ってはいけません。
examples.romaji: koko de shashin o totte wa ikemasen.
examples.english: You must not take photos here.

scenario.setting: A museum gallery — a visitor raises their phone.

lines.speaker: Visitor
lines.japanese: すみません、ここ写真撮っていいですか。
lines.romaji: sumimasen, koko shashin totte ii desu ka.
lines.english: Excuse me, is it okay to take photos here?

lines.speaker: Staff
lines.japanese: 申し訳ありません、展示の保護のため…
lines.romaji: moushiwake arimasen, tenji no hogo no tame…
lines.english: I'm sorry — to protect the exhibits…

examples.japanese: 廊下を走ってはいけない。
examples.english: You must not run in the hallway.

scenario.setting: An elementary school hallway between classes.

lines.speaker: Student
lines.english: Teacher, I'm going to be late!

examples.japanese: 宿題を忘れてはいけません。
examples.english: You must not forget your homework.

scenario.setting: A teacher reminds the class at the end of the lesson.

lines.speaker: Student
lines.japanese: 明日、何持ってきたらいいですか。
lines.romaji: ashita, nani motte kitara ii desu ka.

lines.speaker: Teacher
lines.japanese: ノートはいいですが、大事なのは…
lines.romaji: nooto wa ii desu ga, daiji na no wa…
lines.english: A notebook is fine, but what's important is…

drills.exampleJapanese: ここでタバコを吸ってはいけません。

drills.correctChoice: そこに行ってはいけない

drills.prompt: You must not take photos here.
choices: ここで写真を撮ってはいけません。
ここで写真を撮ってもいいです。
ここで写真を撮りましょう。
drills.correctChoice: ここで写真を撮ってはいけません。

formation.title: From the negative ない-stem
formation.body:
Take the verb's negative stem (ない-form without ない) and add ちゃ or きゃ.

いく → いかない → いかなくちゃ

formation.title: Short forms
formation.body: なくちゃ and なきゃ often stand alone as "gotta / have to." You can add いけない for emphasis.

usage.title: Casual obligation
usage.body: Spoken shorthand for なければならない. Used with friends and family.

usage.title: Compared to なければならない
usage.body: Same obligation meaning, but なくちゃ is informal. Avoid in formal writing.

scenario.setting: A friend checks their watch during a hangout.

lines.speaker: B
lines.english: Can't you stay a little longer?

examples.japanese: 薬を飲まなくちゃいけない。
examples.english: I have to take my medicine.

scenario.setting: A parent notices their child skipping evening meds.

lines.speaker: Child
lines.japanese: もう平気だよ。飲まなくていいでしょ。
lines.romaji: mou heiki da yo. nomanakute ii desho.
lines.english: I'm fine now. I don't need to take it, right?

lines.speaker: Parent
lines.japanese: ダメよ。医者が言ったでしょ。
lines.romaji: dame yo. isha ga itta desho.
lines.english: No. The doctor said so, remember?

scenario.setting: Late night — someone is still on the couch scrolling.

lines.speaker: B
lines.japanese: まだ起きてるの？明日早いんでしょ。
lines.romaji: mada okiteru no? ashita hayai n desho.
lines.english: You're still up? You have an early day tomorrow.

points.title: いちばん
points.blurb: Japanese doesn't bolt -est onto adjectives the way English does — it leans on one word that means 'number one.' Drop いちばん in front of almost any adjective or verb phrase and you instantly have a superlative. You'll hear it everywhere from menu descriptions to sports commentary, and once you've got it, you can rank anything.

formation.title: いちばん + い-adjective
formation.body:
Place いちばん directly before the adjective.

この店がいちばん安い。
This shop is the cheapest.

formation.title: いちばん + な-adjective
formation.body:
Same pattern — いちばん comes before the adjective.

彼女がいちばん元気だ。
She is the most energetic.

formation.title: 〜の中でいちばん
formation.body:
Add の中で before いちばん to say 'the most among ~.'

クラスの中でいちばん背が高い。
The tallest in the class.

usage.title: Superlative
usage.body:
いちばん turns any adjective into its superlative form. Unlike English, the adjective itself doesn't change.

おいしい → いちばんおいしい (most delicious)
速い → いちばん速い (fastest)

usage.title: Ranking among a group
usage.body:
Pair いちばん with 〜の中で to specify the pool you're ranking within.

三つの中でこれがいちばん好き。
Of the three, I like this one the most.

levels.japanese: これがいちばんおいしい
これがいちばんおいしいです
田中さんがいちばん速いです
田中さんがいちばん速くいらっしゃいます
これがいちばん楽しい
これがいちばん楽しいですね
こちらがいちばん楽しゅうございます

examples.japanese: このラーメンがいちばん辛い。

scenario.setting: Two friends study a ramen shop's spice chart, trying to choose.

lines.speaker: B
lines.japanese: どれにする？全部辛そうだけど。
lines.romaji: dore ni suru? zenbu karasou da kedo.
lines.english: Which one are you getting? They all look spicy.

lines.speaker: A
lines.japanese: 辛いの大好きだから、迷う。
lines.english: I love spicy food, so it's hard to choose.

examples.japanese: 三つの中で、春がいちばん好きな季節だ。
examples.romaji: mittsu no naka de, haru ga ichiban sukina kisetsu da.
examples.english: Of the three, spring is my favorite season.

scenario.setting: Two coworkers chat by the window as cherry blossoms drift past.

lines.speaker: A
lines.japanese: 最近、いい天気が続いてるね。
lines.romaji: saikin, ii tenki ga tsuzuiteru ne.
lines.english: The weather's been so nice lately.

lines.speaker: B
lines.romaji: hontou ni. shiki no naka de mo...

examples.japanese: この山道の中で、ここがいちばん景色がいい。
examples.romaji: kono yamamichi no naka de, koko ga ichiban keshiki ga ii.
examples.english: Along this mountain trail, this spot has the best view.

scenario.setting: Two hikers reach a rocky overlook, catching their breath.

lines.speaker: B
lines.japanese: やっと着いた…足が痛い。
lines.english: We finally made it... my legs ache.

examples.japanese: 全部食べたけど、チョコレートケーキがいちばんおいしかった。
examples.romaji: zenbu tabeta kedo, chokoreeto keeki ga ichiban oishikatta.
examples.english: I tried everything, but the chocolate cake was the best.

scenario.setting: Friends walk out of a bakery tasting event, comparing notes.

lines.speaker: B
lines.japanese: 全部よかったけど、やっぱり…
lines.english: They were all good, but honestly...

examples.japanese: クラスの中で田中くんがいちばん足が速い。
examples.romaji: kurasu no naka de tanaka-kun ga ichiban ashi ga hayai.
examples.english: Tanaka is the fastest runner in the class.

scenario.setting: A coach talks to a teacher before a school sports day.

lines.speaker: Coach
lines.japanese: リレーに出せる生徒、誰かいますか。
lines.romaji: riree ni daseru seito, dareka imasu ka.
lines.english: Do you have a student who could run the relay?

lines.speaker: Teacher
lines.english: Let me think — if it's about running...

drills.exampleJapanese: このラーメンがいちばん辛い。

drills.prompt: This park is the most beautiful.
choices: この公園がいちばんきれいだ。

この公園はきれいいちばんだ。
この公園がきれいないちばんだ。
drills.correctChoice: この公園がいちばんきれいだ。

drills.exampleJapanese: 三つの中でこの本がいちばん面白い。
choices: Of the three, this book is the most interesting.
This book is more interesting than three others.
I want to read this book the most.
This book is interesting, but not the best.
drills.correctChoice: Of the three, this book is the most interesting.

drills.prompt: Tanaka is the fastest in the class.
choices: 田中くんがクラスでいちばん速い。
田中くんはクラスでもっと速い。
田中くんがクラスで速いです。
田中くんはいちばん速くなりたい。
drills.correctChoice: 田中くんがクラスでいちばん速い。

drills.exampleJapanese: クラスの中でこの問題がいちばん難しかった。
choices: Of all the problems, this one was the hardest.
This problem is harder than the others in class.
I found this problem in class very difficult.
Nobody in class could solve this problem.
drills.correctChoice: Of all the problems, this one was the hardest.

points.title: が①
points.headlineEnglish: subject marker; identifies who or what acts
points.blurb: が marks the subject — who or what does the action. Unlike は, which sets the topic, が spotlights the doer, often answering "who?" or "what?" Use it when you're identifying someone or something for the first time.

formation.title: Noun + が + predicate
formation.body:
Attach が directly to the noun that performs the action.

猫がいる。
There is a cat.

formation.title: Answering 誰が・何が questions
formation.body:
When a question asks 誰が (who) or 何が (what), the answer uses が.

誰が来た？ → 友達が来た。
Who came? → A friend came.

formation.title: が in subordinate clauses
formation.body:
Inside clauses that describe a noun, が is always used — never は.

母が作った料理
The food that Mom made

usage.title: Identifying the subject
usage.body: が points to exactly who or what performs the verb. It often carries a sense of "it is X that —" — highlighting the subject.

usage.title: New information vs. known topic
usage.body:
Use が when the subject is new or being identified. Once established, は often takes over.

犬が来た。犬は大きい。
A dog came. The dog is big.

usage.title: Compared to は
usage.body: は introduces a topic the listener can follow. が identifies the subject. 私は学生です is a self-introduction; 私が学生です singles you out among others.

levels.japanese: 電話が鳴っております

examples.english: There is a cat in the garden.

scenario.setting: Two siblings look out into the yard.

examples.romaji: dare ga kita? tomodachi ga kita.

scenario.setting: Someone hears the doorbell and asks who is visiting.
Two friends step outside and feel raindrops.
A child sees a large dog on a walk.
A phone rings while two people are talking.

drills.instruction: Select the correct particle to complete the sentence.
Which sentence correctly identifies who came?

choices: I made it. (singling out the speaker as the one who did it)
drills.correctChoice: I made it. (singling out the speaker as the one who did it)

drills.contrastLabel: Identifying who did it vs. stating a topic

points.title: が②
points.blurb: When が sits between two adjectives or short clauses, it means "but" or "however." It connects contrasting ideas — a slightly more formal cousin of けど. Both sides of が describe the same subject.

formation.title: Adjective + が + adjective
formation.body:
Link two contrasting descriptions with が between them.

難しいが、楽しい。
It's difficult, but fun.

usage.title: Soft contrast
usage.body: が② acknowledges a downside, then adds a positive (or vice versa). The second part is the main point you want to land on.

scenario.setting: A student talks about their Japanese class.
Two friends look at a tiny puppy.
Someone tries food at a nice restaurant.

examples.english: Today is cold, but I'm going.

scenario.setting: A friend hesitates before leaving the house.

examples.romaji: hon wa furui ga, suki da.
examples.english: The book is old, but I like it.

scenario.setting: Someone shows a worn book they treasure.

choices: 高いけど、おいしくない。

points.title: か①
points.blurb: か between two nouns means "or" — you're offering a choice. It only works when picking between options, not at the end of a question.

formation.title: A + か + B
formation.body:
Put か between the two choices.

コーヒーかお茶？
Coffee or tea?

usage.title: Offering a choice
usage.body: Use か when presenting two (or more) alternatives. The listener picks one. Often used in casual speech without です.

scenario.setting: A host asks a guest what they'd like to drink.
A shop clerk holds up two items.
Two friends talk about pets.
Friends try to pick a day to meet.
Two travelers decide how to get to the station.

lines.speaker: B
lines.english: How do we get to the station?

points.title: か②
points.blurb: か at the end of a sentence turns a statement into a yes/no question. In polite speech you often add ですか. The question mark in English is optional in Japanese — か already signals a question.

formation.title: Statement + か
formation.body:
Add か to the end of a sentence to ask a yes/no question.

雨ですか。
Is it raining?

formation.title: Polite questions
formation.body:
With です or ます, か becomes ですか or ますか.

学生ですか。
Are you a student?

usage.title: Yes/no questions
usage.body: か asks whether something is true. The listener answers はい or いいえ (or a fuller response).

scenario.setting: Someone looks out the window and isn't sure.
A new acquaintance asks about someone's job.
A teacher holds up an object in class.

lines.speaker: B
lines.english: What do you think this is?

scenario.setting: A child asks about an animal at the zoo.
Someone needs to catch a train.

examples.romaji: kawaii onna no ko ga iru.

examples.japanese: 東京まで、３０分くらいです。
早く寝たけれども、まだ眠たいです。
examples.romaji: hayaku neta keredomo, mada nemutai desu.
examples.english: I slept early, but I'm still sleepy.
What do you want to eat?

examples.japanese: 高い肉を食べたことがある。
examples.romaji: takai niku o tabeta koto ga aru.
examples.english: I have eaten expensive meat before.
I plan to go to Japan.

points.title: で①
points.blurb: で marks where an action happens — the stage, not the destination. With 行く you use に (where you're headed); with 食べる or 勉強する you use で (where you do it).

formation.title: Place + で + action verb
formation.body:
Attach で to the location where the action takes place.

学校で勉強する。
To study at school.

usage.title: Action location vs. destination
usage.body: 駅に行く = heading to the station. 駅で待つ = waiting at the station. に is the pin on the map you're moving toward; で is the room you're already acting in.

scenario.setting: A student explains their daily routine.
Friends decide where to have dinner.
Two friends plan to meet before a trip.
Children talk about what to do after school.
Tourists find a good spot for a picture.

drills.instruction: Select the correct particle to complete the sentence.

points.title: で②
points.blurb: で also marks the tool or means — how you get something done. Think "by bus," "with chopsticks," or "in Japanese."

formation.title: Means + で
formation.body:
Put で after the tool, vehicle, or method.

バスで帰る。
To go home by bus.

usage.title: Instrument or method
usage.body: で answers "how?" or "with what?" — the bus you ride, the language you speak, the chopsticks you eat with.

scenario.setting: Someone chooses how to get home after school.
Friends plan a day trip.
A visitor tries Japanese food for the first time.
A teacher encourages a student during conversation practice.
A family plans a weekend drive.

lines.speaker: B
lines.romaji: densha no hou ga hayai yo.

choices: To go home to the bus.
To go home at the bus.
To go home from the bus.

examples.japanese: 映画を見てから、帰ります。
examples.english: After watching the movie, I'll go home.

points.title: に・へ
points.blurb: Both に and へ mark direction — where something is headed. に is more common in everyday speech; へ sounds slightly more literary but means the same thing for destinations.

formation.title: Place + に / へ + movement verb
formation.body:
Either particle works before verbs like 行く and 帰る.

駅に行く。駅へ行く。
To go to the station.

usage.title: に vs. へ
usage.body: For most learners, に and へ are interchangeable with 行く. へ adds a sense of "toward" and appears more in writing, signs, and announcements.

examples.romaji: eki ni iku. eki e iku.
examples.english: To go to the station. / To go toward the station.

scenario.setting: A teacher explains two ways to say the same thing.

examples.japanese: 学校に行く。学校へ行く。
examples.romaji: gakkou ni iku. gakkou e iku.

scenario.setting: A child leaves for school in the morning.

examples.romaji: ie ni kaeru. ie e kaeru.

scenario.setting: Someone finishes work and heads out.

examples.japanese: 公園に行く。公園へ行く。
examples.romaji: kouen ni iku. kouen e iku.

scenario.setting: Friends plan a weekend outing.

examples.japanese: 東京に行く。東京へ行く。
examples.romaji: toukyou ni iku. toukyou e iku.

scenario.setting: Someone talks about a trip.

lines.speaker: A
lines.english: I want to go to Tokyo.

points.title: に
points.blurb: に marks a point in time, a destination, or a target. It answers "when?", "where to?", and "to whom?" — like pinning something on a map or a calendar.

formation.title: Destination: place + に + 行く
formation.body:
Use に with verbs of movement to show where you're headed.

学校に行く。
To go to school.

formation.title: Time: clock time + に
formation.body:
に marks when something happens.

七時に寝る。
To sleep at seven o'clock.

formation.title: Target: person + に
formation.body:
に can mark who receives an action.

友達に電話する。
To call a friend.

usage.title: Location vs. action
usage.body: に marks where something exists (駅にいる) or where you're headed (駅に行く). For where an action takes place, use で instead.

scenario.setting: A parent asks where a child is headed in the morning.
A parent reminds a child about bedtime.
A student packs up after school.
Someone picks up their phone to make a call.
A friend texts to ask where someone is.

drills.instruction: Select the correct particle to complete the sentence.

choices: To sleep because of seven o'clock.

points.title: にいく
points.headlineEnglish: to go in order to do…

examples.japanese: エレベーターで５かいにいく。
examples.english: To go to the 5th floor by elevator.

examples.romaji: kare wa hashiru no ga hayai.

examples.japanese: 彼は漢字を書くのが下手。
examples.romaji: kare wa kanji o kaku no ga heta.
examples.english: He is bad at writing kanji.

examples.romaji: kanojo wa utau no ga jouzu.
inu to asobu no ga suki.

points.title: ので
points.headlineEnglish: because of; the reason is that

examples.japanese: 太いので、走るのは遅い。
examples.romaji: futoi node, hashiru no wa osoi.
examples.english: Because I'm big, I'm slow at running.

points.title: は
points.blurb: は marks the topic of your sentence — what you're talking about. Think of it as setting the stage: "As for X…" The rest of the sentence tells us something about that topic. It doesn't mean "is" on its own.

formation.title: Noun + は
formation.body:
Place は right after the word you want to talk about.

私は学生です。
As for me, (I) am a student.

usage.title: Topic, not subject
usage.body: は frames what the sentence is about. The verb or adjective that follows describes that topic — not necessarily the doer of an action.

usage.title: Compared to が
usage.body: が identifies who or what acts ("a cat came"). は picks up a topic you keep talking about ("the cat is small").

scenario.setting: Two classmates introduce themselves on the first day of school.
A student holds up something from their bag.
Two friends look out the window in the morning.
A child points at a kitten in the park.

examples.romaji: haha wa ryouri ga suki desu.

scenario.setting: Someone talks about their family at dinner.

drills.instruction: Select the correct particle to complete the sentence.

choices: I want to be a student.

points.title: も
points.blurb: も means "also" or "too" — it adds something to the set. Unlike は, which sets a topic, も layers on: "this too," "me too," "also at school."

formation.title: Noun + も
formation.body:
Replace は or が with も to add "also."

私も学生です。
I am also a student.

usage.title: Adding to a group
usage.body: も includes the marked item in whatever was already mentioned. 猫が好き。犬も好き。 = I like cats. I like dogs too.
